title: Mitigating Privacy Risks in Graph Condensation from a Hyperbolic Geometry Perspective

problem.claim: Graph condensation may create privacy leakage while seeking efficient training and model generalization.

gap.claim: It remains unclear whether common membership inference attack accuracy adequately represents graph-condensation privacy, whether condensation is robust to stronger adversaries, and why it performs as observed.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes HDGC, a graph-condensation framework that studies privacy issues from a hyperbolic geometric perspective.
HDGC constrains gradient-matching directions with hyperbolic geometric properties to obtain hierarchical semantic guidance for learning synthetic graph topology and to measure node importance.

HDGC introduces hyperbolic adaptive differentially private noise during gradient matching and uses distributionally robust optimization to reduce utility degradation from noise while preserving privacy guarantees.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly describe HDGC as a novel graph-condensation framework based on a hyperbolic geometric perspective.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that existing methods often trade performance and generalization, and that increased node diversity can amplify privacy leakage.
The authors report that HDGC captures geometric-space characteristics, achieves superior performance, and provides a foundation for defending inference attacks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph condensation creates smaller synthetic graphs for efficient training and potential privacy protection.
The adequacy of common membership inference attacks, robustness to stronger adversaries, and reasons for observed performance remain unresolved.
Tailored attacks are used to investigate privacy risks, revealing tensions among performance, generalization, node diversity, and privacy leakage.
HDGC combines hyperbolic gradient-direction constraints, adaptive differential privacy noise, and distributionally robust optimization.
The authors report improved performance and a foundation for defending inference attacks.

source_observation.claim: Increasing node diversity may improve generalization but can increase privacy leakage and attack reasoning due to greater data disparity.

interpretation.claim: Utility, generalization, diversity, and privacy should be evaluated as coupled objectives rather than optimized independently.

application.claim: When designing synthetic-data methods, assess stronger or tailored inference attacks alongside task performance and generalization.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that this trade-off applies beyond the described graph-condensation setting.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide dataset details, baseline identities, quantitative results, attack accuracies, or experimental settings.
The abstract does not specify the formal privacy budget, optimization procedure, or proof details for the privacy guarantees.
The abstract does not independently verify the reported performance or inference-attack defense claims.
